name: Dusty steel blue
lede: Dusty steel blue renders Gunjō-iro (群青色), the traditional Japanese name for ultramarine, the blue ground from the mineral azurite.

sections.title: Named for a mineral pigment
sections.body:
Our color library gives the source as 群青色 (Gunjō-iro), "ultramarine color": gunjō is the Japanese name for the blue pigment ground from azurite, long used in Japanese painting for mountains and water [1]. No first-recorded date survives in our sources, so when the name entered use is undocumented here [1]. The modern swatch here is a greyed, muted blue, considerably softer than the saturated blue the mineral pigment itself produces [1].

The nearest named color in our graph is [[brittany]], at a color distance (ΔE2000) of 2.7, almost the same shade; [[steel-blue]] itself sits 5.0 away and reads more vivid and bluer [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this blue in 116 of 23,781 paintings, about 0.5 percent, as photographed [3]. It peaks in the 1510s (7 of 243 paintings from that decade), and Claude Monet and Paul Cezanne each carry it at more than twelve times the overall rate, with Post-Impressionist painting generally running at nine times the average [3]. France holds the largest share by country, and the earliest dated match is Marco Zoppo's *Madonna and Child* (1467), a floor set by what survives and was photographed, not a first appearance [3]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings; the match is computed, not a pigment identification [3].

questions.q: What mineral pigment does the Japanese name behind Dusty steel blue, Gunjō-iro, name?
True or false: the modern swatch for Dusty steel blue is as saturated as the mineral pigment ultramarine.

openers: Dusty steel blue's name points to ultramarine, a mineral pigment far more saturated than this greyed swatch.
